# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the management of severe aortic stenosis, with randomized trials establishing its non-inferiority or superiority to surgery across the spectrum of surgical risk. On the basis of a rate of death from any cause at 1 year that was 20 percentage points lower with TAVI than with standard therapy, balloon-expandable TAVI should be the new standard of care for patients with aortic stenosis who are not suitable candidates for surgery [1], with subsequent trials extending benefit to high- and intermediate-risk populations [2,3]. The transfemoral artery remains the default access route [4], yet a meaningful minority of patients have iliofemoral vessels that are too small, tortuous, or calcified to accommodate large-bore sheaths. Transfemoral access may not be feasible in 10-15% of the candidate patients for TAVI due to severe peripheral arterial disease or unfavorable iliofemoral anatomy [5]. Transcaval access emerged to serve precisely this population.

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval access entails delivering a large introducer sheath from the femoral vein, across the inferior vena cava (IVC), into the adjoining abdominal aorta. An alternative access route to the abdominal aorta for large-vessel introducer sheaths is direct puncture from the adjoining inferior vena cava; the veins are larger and more compliant than corresponding arteries, and venous decompression may avert hemorrhage [6]. The counterintuitive safety of intentionally puncturing the aorta is explained by retroperitoneal mechanics: although counterintuitive, its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole [7]. The technique was first validated preclinically in 2013 [6].

## First-in-Human Experience and Technique

The first human series was reported in 2014. Between July 2013 and January 2014, 19 patients underwent TAVR via caval-aortic access; caval-aortic access and tract closure were successful in all 19 patients, and TAVR was successful in 17 [8]. Procedurally, access is obtained by directing an electrified guidewire from the IVC into a snare prepositioned in the aorta, followed by guidewire exchange, sheath advancement, retrograde TAVR, and closure of the aorto-caval tract with a nitinol occluder [9,10]. Electrosurgical wire traversal is now recognized as a core enabling principle of these procedures [11]. Careful computed tomographic (CT) planning is essential to select a calcium-free infrarenal crossing target [12,13].

## Prospective and Registry Evidence

A prospective, multicenter NHLBI investigational device exemption trial enrolled 100 patients ineligible for both transfemoral and transthoracic access. Transcaval access was successful in 99 of 100 subjects, and device success was 98 of 99 [14]. Transcaval access enabled TAVR in patients who were not good candidates for transthoracic access; bleeding and vascular complications, using permeable nitinol cardiac occluders to close the access ports, were common but acceptable in this high-risk cohort [14]. One-year follow-up demonstrated favorable healing of access tracts on serial CT [15,16]. The initial European multicenter registry reinforced these findings: transcaval access was successful in 49 out of 50 patients and device success was obtained in 94% of cases [17], and transfemoral transcaval access proved to be a feasible and safe TAVI approach for high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis not suitable for transfemoral or transaxillary/subclavian transarterial access [17].

Comparative data are also encouraging. In a propensity-weighted analysis of TVT Registry centers, transcaval access had a lower rate of stroke/TIA than transaxillary access for TAVR, comparable bleeding and vascular complications, and a higher rate of discharge directly to home without stroke/TIA [18]. A 2025 meta-analysis concluded that the transcaval approach is feasible and non-inferior to other alternative accesses in TAVI patients with prohibitive iliofemoral anatomy [19].

## Closure and Refinements

Bleeding from the access site has been the principal limitation, historically addressed with off-label nitinol cardiac occluders [14,16]. A purpose-built solution has since been tested: this study sought to test safety and exploratory effectiveness of a dedicated transcaval closure device [20], with first-in-human results suggesting simplified closure and reduced bleeding [20,21]. Best-practice consensus statements now address CT planning, electrosurgery technique, and pacing strategy; for example, femoral transvenous pacemakers are best placed after the transcaval TAVR sheath, to avoid inadvertent advancement by the transcaval sheath [22].

## Expanding Applications

Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has broadened to other large-bore needs. Transcaval access has been performed in thousands of patients for transcatheter aortic valve replacement and endovascular thoracic aneurysm repair and to avoid limb ischemia in percutaneous mechanical circulatory support [22]. The first thoracic endovascular aneurysm repair via transcaval access was reported when pelvic arteries were inadequate [23], and the route has enabled access across synthetic aortic grafts [24,25]. In cardiogenic shock, transcaval aortic access is a percutaneous technique to deliver large-bore catheter devices from a femoral vein into the abdominal aorta in patients with inadequate peripheral arterial access; in this setting, it may enable VA-ECMO in patients with diseased iliofemoral arteries [26]. Special populations including those undergoing concomitant electrosurgical leaflet modification (BASILICA/LAMPOON) [27,28] and morbidly obese patients [29] have also been treated, underscoring the procedure's versatility within contemporary structural heart practice [30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access is an established, fully percutaneous alternative for delivering large-bore devices to the aorta when transfemoral access is precluded. Accumulating prospective, registry, and meta-analytic evidence supports its feasibility and acceptable safety, and dedicated closure technology promises to narrow the gap with transfemoral outcomes. Broader dissemination will depend on commercial device availability, structured training, and continued comparative study.
